title: 383. The Zoo I Built
author: By Title Only
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (bytitleonly.substack.com), August 10, 2026
summary: Using an extended, seven-animal metaphor, the author of By Title Only diagnoses a dysfunctional leadership team through the exact traits that made each member attractive at the hiring stage: the loyal but alarm-prone Dog, the self-motivated but unmanageable Cat, the visionary but ground-blind Giraffe, the protective but unreachable Porcupine, the resourceful but credit-stealing Raccoon, the institutional-memory-rich but change-blocking Elephant, and the slow-to-hire but crisis-steady Sloth. The essay's real turn comes in its final section, where the author admits the zoo isn't an accident of bad hiring but a mirror of their own leadership: 'I didn't just hire these traits, I promoted the exact traits that now drive me crazy,' and 'the team is anxious because I'm anxious.' The piece closes by reframing each animal not as a fixed personality type to manage around but as a mode any leader (including the author) can slip into situationally — the real skill isn't hiring the right animal, it's noticing which animal you're being in the moment and choosing a better one when it matters, and building a team that draws on each animal's strength rather than assembling, unintentionally, a food chain.
points: The essay's sharpest insight is the reversal at the end: the animals aren't hiring mistakes, they're a mirror — 'I didn't just hire these traits, I promoted the exact traits that now drive me crazy' — reframing team dysfunction as a leadership-culture problem rather than a personnel problem.

Each animal pairs a genuine strength with its shadow cost in the same trait (the Dog's loyalty is inseparable from his inability to distinguish real threats from noise; the Porcupine's protectiveness is inseparable from being impossible to give feedback to), modeling how leaders should evaluate candidates' weaknesses as the flip side of their strengths, not separately from them.

'The team is anxious because I'm anxious... they stopped bringing me new ideas because they saw what happens to new ideas when I hear them' names a specific, common leadership failure mode: a leader's own reactivity training the team to stop surfacing information.

The closing reframe — that the best leaders aren't a fixed animal but can 'sense which animal they're being, and pick a better one when it matters' — turns a fun team-typing exercise into an actionable self-monitoring practice for the reader's own leadership moments.

The best leaders aren't necessarily a particular animal. They're the ones who can sense which animal they're being, and pick a better one when it matters.
